content: Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) refers to a collection of health issues that are directly associated with an individual's workplace environment, most commonly office buildings, though it can also occur in residential settings. A 1984 report by the World Health Organization estimated that up to 30% of newly constructed or renovated buildings worldwide might be linked to symptoms of SBS. The primary causes of SBS are often attributed to deficiencies in heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems. These issues are frequently resolved by increasing the rate of fresh air exchange with outdoor air. Other contributing factors include the release of contaminants from certain building materials, inadequate exhaust ventilation for light industrial chemicals used indoors, and microbial contamination. Symptoms of SBS Individuals affected by SBS may experience a wide range of symptoms, including: Headaches. Irritation of the eyes, nose, or throat. Dry cough or dry, itchy skin. Dizziness and nausea. Difficulty concentrating. Fatigue. Heightened sensitivity to odors. Increased frequency of asthma attacks or the onset of asthma in individuals without a prior history. Personality changes, such as episodes of rage, crying, paranoia, or depression. Cases resembling bronchitis or pneumonia that do not respond to antibiotic treatment. Symptoms similar to Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). This list is not exhaustive, as over 50 potential symptoms have been identified. It is common for multiple occupants of a building to report a diverse array of symptoms, which may initially appear unrelated. The key to identifying SBS lies in recognizing a noticeable increase in illnesses that begin or worsen within a relatively short time frame, often within weeks. Some experts argue that symptoms must resolve shortly after leaving the building for SBS to be diagnosed, but this perspective overlooks the lingering effects of neurotoxins, which may persist even after exposure ends. In particularly sensitive individuals, long-term health consequences are a significant concern. Causes of SBS The factors contributing to SBS are often linked to the design and maintenance of the built environment. These may include: Indoor air pollution. Toxic mold. Artificial fragrances, such as those from dryer sheets. Poor or inappropriate lighting, including limited access to natural sunlight. Inadequate heating or ventilation. Microbial or mite contamination within HVAC systems. Emissions from office equipment, such as computer monitors and photocopiers. Poor ergonomic design. Chemical contamination. Biological contamination. For building owners or operators, the consequences of SBS may manifest as high rates of employee illness or absenteeism, reduced productivity, low job satisfaction, and high employee turnover. Prevention of SBS Preventative measures to address SBS include: Removing or modifying pollutant sources, such as proper storage of chemicals. Replacing water-damaged ceiling tiles and carpeting. Implementing smoking restrictions. Using paints, adhesives, solvents, and pesticides in well-ventilated areas and during periods when the building is unoccupied. Ensuring at least four air exchanges per 24-hour period. Conducting proper and frequent maintenance of HVAC systems. By addressing these factors, the risk of SBS can be significantly reduced, improving both the health of building occupants and overall workplace productivity.
